description: The question's literal reading is wrong. Its reading in the conversation is right. Earlier turns establish the setting, a web app where each request is a separate process. The last message says Python cannot pause at a line and resume there. Generators can pause and resume within a single process. In this setting they cannot, because a suspended generator does not survive a process boundary. A good answer affirms the user's claim within that setting.

history.content: I'm building a web app on top of LangGraph. The graph runs inside request handlers, and each request is handled by a separate worker process; nothing in memory survives from one request to the next. I want to use LangGraph's human-in-the-loop feature so the graph can stop, ask the user something, and continue once they answer in a later request.

That fits LangGraph's interrupt() with a checkpointer: the graph state is saved when it stops, and a later request resumes it from the saved checkpoint. Since each request is its own process, the checkpointer has to be a persistent one (Postgres, Redis, or similar), not the in-memory saver.

input.task: Right, and that's why the human-in-the-loop feature cannot pause at a specific line in my node and resume from that exact line. Python doesn't have the ability to do that. Correct?
